segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy ones, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, their Lord and ours:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I give thanks to my God always for you, because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that in everything you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as the testimony about Christ was firmly established among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you are not lacking in any gift as you eagerly await the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He will also establish you firmly to the end, beyond accusation on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it has been made clear to me about you, my brothers and sisters, by Chloe’s people, that there are quarrels among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: each of you is saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Christ.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Has Christ been divided up? Paul was not crucified for you, was he? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I give thanks that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to announce the good news, and not with wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied of its power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the intelligence of the intelligent I will set aside.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to the called themselves, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God’s foolishness is wiser than human beings, and God’s weakness is stronger than human beings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For consider your calling, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame what is strong,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and God chose what is lowborn in the world and what is despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no flesh may boast before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But it is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

notes.note: In ordinary Greek this word meant a gathering of people, especially a city’s citizen assembly, and the Septuagint uses it for the gathered congregation of Israel. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, which the word did not. Most translations keep “church”, and it is not in doubt that the Christian community is meant.

The word is the ordinary adjective “holy” used as a noun for people set apart as belonging to God, and Paul applies it to every member of the community. “Saints” now suggests a special class of exceptionally virtuous or canonized individuals. The rendering also keeps the link with “made holy” earlier in the verse, which comes from the same root.

The Greek says only “theirs and ours”, placed directly after “in every place”. Most interpreters take it with “our Lord” (he is their Lord as well as ours), and the translation supplies “Lord” to make that explicit. It could instead be read with “place”: “in every place, theirs and ours”.

The word means sharing, partnership or common participation. The phrase can mean companionship with the Son or a share in the Son and what belongs to him, and many scholars think Paul intends the second, stronger sense. The translation keeps the traditional wording, which leaves both open.

notes.traditional: those of the household of Chloe
notes.note: The Greek is simply “those of Chloe”, a normal way of referring to members of a household: slaves, freed dependants or business agents. Chloe is otherwise unknown, and it is not certain whether she herself was a believer or whether she lived in Corinth or in Ephesus, where Paul was writing.

Cephas is the Aramaic name, meaning “rock”, of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul normally uses the Aramaic form. The slogans are literally “I am of Paul” and so on, a way of declaring allegiance.

Many manuscripts read “I give thanks to God”. The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading found in some important early manuscripts, which copyists are more likely to have expanded than abbreviated. The sense is not affected.

notes.phrase: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 29:14 in its Greek form, with one change: where the Septuagint has “I will hide” the intelligence of the intelligent, Paul has “I will set aside”. The verb “destroy” is the same Greek verb as “perishing” in verse 18, a link English cannot easily show.

In Jewish usage the word meant a trained expert in Scripture and its law; in Greek cities it could also name a civic official. “Scribe” now suggests a mere copyist, which is not the point here. Many commentators think Paul has the Jewish legal expert specifically in view, set beside the Greek “wise person”.

The Greek is literally “according to the flesh”, where “flesh” stands for ordinary human existence and its ways of measuring worth. The literal phrase is opaque in modern English and can wrongly suggest the body or sensuality. In verse 29 the same word is kept in the Semitic idiom “no flesh”, meaning no human being.

notes.phrase: and righteousness and holiness and redemption
notes.traditional: and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption
notes.note: The Greek can be read as four parallel things Christ became, or as “wisdom” explained by the three terms that follow (wisdom, that is, righteousness, holiness and redemption). Many scholars prefer the second reading; the translation leaves both open. “Holiness”, traditionally “sanctification”, is from the same root as “made holy” and “holy ones” in verse 2.

notes.phrase: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord
notes.note: This is a condensed form of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Septuagint), where those who boast are told to boast not in wisdom, strength or wealth but in knowing the Lord. The wise, the powerful and the well-born of verse 26 echo that passage. Paul cites the same line in 2 Corinthians 10:17.

candidates.reason: Occurs over a hundred times across the New Testament, and the choice between “church”, “assembly” and “congregation” must be uniform or readers will think different things are meant.
The substantive use for believers recurs throughout the letters and Revelation, and “saints” versus “holy ones” or “God’s people” needs one decision.
Paul uses it in several senses (body, humanity, human standards, the sinful sphere), and translators differ sharply on when to keep “flesh”, so the senses need register entries.
Frequent in the Gospels and Acts, where “scribe” misleads modern readers, so the rendering here should match whatever is chosen there.
A favourite Pauline verb variously rendered “abolish”, “nullify”, “destroy” and “bring to nothing”; without a decision its recurrence across the letters will be hidden.
